points: 1 Scope and problem: the report covers only Koren's predictors added since the 2008 Progress Prize report to the winning 'BellKor's Pragmatic Chaos' Netflix Grand Prize solution. These are improved time-aware baseline predictors, timeSVD++ built on them, a time-aware item-item neighborhood model, RBMs with conditional visible units, and GBDT blending (p. 1).

2 Data and evaluation setup: >100M dated ratings, 480,189 users, 17,770 movies. The ~4.2M-rating Hold-out set (each user's last nine ratings) is split into Probe, Quiz and Test. Every reported RMSE is on Quiz, and Netflix never disclosed Test scores (p. 1).

3 Tuning: constants are set by a manual greedy search on Probe, never revisited, and shared across variants. The author accepts this as suboptimal because over-tuning one predictor adds little to the blend (pp. 1-2). The only automatic tuning (APT1) is on baseline (11), with log base a=6.76, and gained just 0.0016 RMSE (p. 4).

4 Time-aware baseline mechanism and results: item bias in 30 time bins of about 10 weeks; user bias = bu + αu·devu(t) (β=0.4) + day-specific bu,t; plus a scaling cu(t) on the item bias. RMSE is 0.9605 for (9) and 0.9555 for (10), against Cinematch's 0.9514 (pp. 2-3).

5 Frequency term: fui=⌊log_a Fui⌋ (idea from Pragmatic Theory) enters as an item×frequency bias bi,fui. It lowers baseline RMSE from 0.9555 to 0.9278, significantly better than Cinematch. Most of the benefit disappears in full models with interaction terms. The explanation (biased selection in bulk rating) is a hypothesis (pp. 3-4).

6 timeSVD++: time-dependent user factors (eq. 14/15) and frequency-aware model (16). Results range from 0.8914 (f=20) to a best of 0.8762 (f=2000); [PQ2] is 0.8777. Frequency-specific movie factors were 'barely beneficial'. Over-training beyond 40 iterations helps the blend (p. 5).

7 Time-aware neighborhood: global item-item weights wij, cij with a user-specific exponential time decay e^(-βu·Δt). RMSE improves from 0.9002 (static) to 0.8870 [PQ3], and the step from 0.8885 to 0.8870 is attributed to the frequency bias. The paper claims this beats hybrid neighborhood results (p. 6).

8 RBMs with visible units conditioned on user, user×date and movie×frequency biases. Eq. (20) variants give 0.8942-0.8952. The frequency RBM gives 0.8928, 'the best we know' for a pure RBM. Day-specific hidden units give 0.9060 [PQ6], 'not encouraging' (pp. 7-8).

9 GBDT blending: trained on Probe and applied to Qualifying, with extra features (user support, movie support, frequency, date). Results: 454 predictors 0.8603, 75 predictors 0.8606, 24 BellKor predictors 0.8664 (p. 8).

10 GBDT extensions and assessment: adding timeSVD++ factors gives 0.8661, RBM user units 0.8661, kNN features 0.8660. Per-movie GBDT on RBM units [PQ7] gives 0.9248. GBDT accuracy lags the neural-network blenders and its impact was smaller than hoped (pp. 8-9).

errors.quote: User bias has three parts: a drift term αu·sign(t−tu)|t−tu|^β with β = 0.4, a per-user-day term but, and a per-user-day scale cu(t) multiplying the item bias.
errors.paper: The user bias (8) is bu + αu·devu(t) + bu,t. cu(t) = cu + cut is a separate 'time-dependent scaling feature' that multiplies the item bias in (10). It is not part of the user bias (p. 3).

errors.quote: GBDT blending, results ... | blend of predictors 2, 9, 12, 13 | 0.8713 (p. 9) |
errors.paper: The 0.8713 predictor is not a GBDT blend. It 'is based on the blending technique described in page 12 of [3]', applied to predictors 2, 9, 12, 13 (p. 9).

errors.quote: It says most of the gain disappears once interaction terms are added; this is an argument, not a measured result
errors.paper: The paper presents this as one of 'two empirical observations': frequencies 'contribute much less within a full method, where most of their benefit disappears when adding the user-movie interaction terms' (p. 3). The neighborhood result supports it with a measurement (0.8885→0.8870, p. 6).

errors.quote: Eq. (16) ranges from 0.8777 (f = 200, 40 iterations, called [PQ2]) to 0.8762 (f = 2000, 40 iterations)

best.why: C covers all ten points with a single minor range slip. It also adds the most useful context for answering questions: GBDT hyperparameters, the 40-rating-days figure, the Quiz set's role in choosing RBM iteration counts, a flag on unsupported claims, and a warning about garbled equations.
